st.headline: Young bankers to manage AI agents from start, Goldman exec says
st.teaser: It raised the question of what happens to the current middle managers.
fullText: SINGAPORE – The newest hires in finance will not have to wait years to become managers. They will be overseeing artificial intelligence agents from the time they join, raising the question of what happens to the current middle managers, according to Goldman Sachs Group’s Kevin Sneader.

“When our young folks now start work, they’re managing agents,” Sneader, who leads the Wall Street bank’s business in Asia Pacific outside Japan, said on Oct 8 at the Milken Institute Asia Summit in Singapore.
“They have to make the most of this virtual army that they’ve now got.”
Previous generations often spent years in the job before they got to manage anyone, and re-deploying these managers will be the “generational challenge for many, many segments”, he added.

His comments suggest AI could upend the traditional banking career path, where junior staff spend years on analysis and preparatory work before moving up to manage others. Rather than fretting about mass job losses due to the technology, Sneader and others speaking on a panel about AI and finance were focused on how roles would be reshaped.
“That management task no longer sits with the middle manager; it sits with the front line,” Sneader said. “We don’t quite know what’s going to happen to that group.”
Sandra Peterson, an operating partner at investment firm Clayton, Dubilier & Rice, said the traditional career ladder may not survive.

“It used to be that professional service firms were pyramids,” she said. “You’d show up, and you know, you march your way through, and if you survived, you got to the next level, the next level, the next level.”
She said that with AI doing much of the grunt work, it is not clear firms would need as many entry-level positions.

Singapore’s financial regulator sees the same shifts happening. Operations staff will need to become managers and supervisors of AI agents, Chia Der Jiun, managing director of the Monetary Authority of Singapore, said at the same panel.
Banks will also need fewer fresh graduates for analysis and preparatory work, he said.
The city-state has been preparing for these changes through training bank staff in AI skills as well as working with the universities to ensure its graduates are ready for the new world, Chia said.
For young people however, Sneader said the upside goes beyond angling for a finance job.
“There’s never been a better time to be an entrepreneur to create something,” he said, noting that fewer resources are needed to start a business nowadays.
“That’s quite an exciting part of the future when we’re all spending too much time, perhaps worrying about the old world.” BLOOMBERG

cna.headline: France's Sesterce plans $11 billion AI investment in Finland
cna.teaser: France's Sesterce plans $11 billion AI investment in Finland
fullText: OSLO, Oct 8 : French AI infrastructure group Sesterce said on Thursday it plans to develop a data centre site in Finland costing more than €10 billion ($11.21 billion), the latest in a series of foreign technology investments in the Nordic country.
• The first phase, with works planned to start in 2026, will have a capacity of 200 megawatt (MW), Sesterce said in a statement
• Capacity is expected to increase to 600 MW in the second phase
• The company said it already has an anchor customer for the project, which will be built in Jamsa in central Finland at the site of a former paper mill that closed in 2021

listening.title: The Greening of HDB Estates
listening.transcript: As Singapore strives to achieve net-zero emissions, housing estates are undergoing a massive transformation. Older public housing blocks are being retrofitted with solar panels, smart LED lights, and urban farming spaces on rooftops. Residents are also encouraged to participate in community-led recycling programs. These localized green initiatives not only reduce energy bills but also foster a stronger sense of environmental stewardship among neighbors.

economistArticle.title: Why shares are the new bricks and mortar
paras: For decades, real estate was the undisputed king of wealth accumulation, particularly in land-scarce Asian hubs like Singapore. Buying a residential home was not just a rite of passage; it was considered the ultimate financial safety net. But a tectonic shift is underway as younger, tech-savvy investors begin to pivot away from illiquid concrete toward highly liquid global equities.

Multiple factors explain this modern migration. Staggering property prices, propelled by stubbornly high interest rates and punitive stamp duties aimed at cooling the market, have effectively priced out a whole generation of potential homeowners. To purchase a decent condominium today requires an intimidating capital outlay. In contrast, fractional shares and low-cost exchange-traded funds (ETFs) offer a friction-free, instantly accessible entry point into global markets.

Furthermore, the psychological appeal of physical property has waned. Where older generations saw stability in brick and mortar, modern professionals see handcuffs. Owning an expensive home limits geographic mobility and locks up massive amounts of capital that could otherwise compound dynamically in international technology stocks or high-yield index funds.

Financial institutions are quickly adapting to this cultural evolution. Robo-advisors and digital brokerage platforms have democratized equity investment, making portfolio diversification as simple as a few taps on a smartphone. This ease of access has demystified Wall Street for the average saver, who now views stock indices as a much more agile wealth generator than a heavily leveraged, thirty-year mortgage.

Ultimately, this transition from real estate to equities represents a maturation of household finance. While physical property will always retain its emotional resonance as a sanctuary, the future of wealth creation lies in the fluidity of capital markets. For the modern investor, financial security is no longer built of stone, but forged in the digital ledger.
economistArticle.cn:
几十年来，房地产一直是毫无争议的财富积累之王，特别是在像新加坡这样土地稀缺的亚洲枢纽。购买住宅不仅仅是一种成年礼，它还被视为终极的财务安全网。但随着年轻的、精通科技的投资者开始从流动性差的混凝土房产转向流动性强的全球股票，一场结构性的转变正在发生。

有多种因素可以解释这一现代迁移。在高利率和旨在降温市场的惩罚性印花税的推动下，令人咂舌的房价实际上将整整一代潜在购房者拒之门外。如今，购买一套像样的公寓需要令人望而生畏的资金支出。相比之下，零碎股和低成本交易所交易基金（ETF）为进入全球市场提供了一个无摩擦、可即时获取的切入点。

此外，实体房产在心理上的吸引力已经减弱。老一辈人在砖瓦房产中看到了稳定，而现代专业人士却看到了枷锁。拥有一套昂贵的房子限制了地理上的流动性，并锁住了大量资金，而这些资金本可以在国际科技股或高收益指数基金中进行动态复利增长。

金融机构正迅速适应这种文化演变。智能投顾和数字经纪平台使股权投资走入平民百姓家，使投资组合多元化变得像在智能手机上轻点几下一样简单。这种便捷的获取方式为普通储户揭开了华尔街的神秘面纱，他们现在认为股票指数比高杠杆的三十年期抵押贷款是更灵活的财富生成器。

最终，这种从房地产到股票的转变代表了家庭财务的成熟。虽然实体房产作为避风港将始终保持其情感共鸣，但财富创造的未来在于资本市场的流动性。对于现代投资者而言，财务安全不再由石头筑成，而是在数字账本中锻造而成。

gems.s: Where older generations saw stability in brick and mortar, modern professionals see handcuffs.
gems.why: This sentence uses a beautifully balanced contrast structure ('Where older... modern professionals see...') alongside the metaphorical noun 'handcuffs' to turn an abstract financial attitude shift into a vivid and memorable physical image. 这句话运用了对称的对比结构（‘在旧一代人看到……的地方，现代专业人士却看到了……’），并巧妙地使用了隐喻词‘手铐/枷锁’，将抽象的财务观念转变塑造成一个生动且令人难忘的视觉形象。
